report:
### Conclusion
Your impression is supported by recent high-quality evidence: taking probiotics generally does **not** shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea.

### Evidence
* **Updated Cochrane Review (2020):** While earlier reviews suggested minor benefits, the updated Cochrane systematic review incorporated large, rigorous trials with a low risk of bias. It concluded that probiotics probably make little or no difference to the proportion of people experiencing diarrhea lasting 48 hours or longer, and there is uncertainty regarding whether they reduce overall duration (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/).
* **Major Clinical Trials:** Large randomized controlled trials published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* demonstrated that probiotic formulations showed no significant clinical benefit over placebo in treating children with acute gastroenteritis (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597).
* **Expert Guidelines:** Based on these robust findings, professional organizations such as the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) advise against the routine use of probiotics for acute gastroenteritis (https://agau.gastro.org/course/aga-clinical-guidelines-on-role-of-probiotics-in-the-management-of-gastrointestinal-disorders--educational-webinar/fc00953e-2419-4089-9be6-ee317f241574).
